title: A single river in the sky can carry more water than the Amazon
body: Atmospheric rivers are narrow corridors of water vapour, typically several thousand kilometres long but only a few hundred wide. Between them they carry **over 90%** of the water vapour that moves north and south across the globe, and a single one can carry a greater flow of water than the Amazon, Earth's largest river. When one hits a coast with mountains, the moist air is forced uphill, cools and drops its water as heavy rain and snow, which is why they can end droughts and also cause floods. On the coast of California and the western US, a 2013 study found they bring 30 to 50% of the year's rain.

slides.label: of the water vapour moving north and south through the air travels in atmospheric rivers
slides.text: They are long and thin: thousands of kilometres from end to end, a few hundred across.

slides.heading: How a river in the sky makes rain

steps.label: Winds carry it in a narrow plume
Mountains force the moist air up
The air cools and drops rain and snow

slides.prompt: Atmospheric rivers that carry warm moisture from near Hawaii to the US West Coast have a nickname. What is it?
slides.detail: The name comes from where the plumes start, over the Hawaiian tropics. NASA says this kind of rain provides about 40% of California's yearly water supply.

slides.question: About how many atmospheric rivers flow in each hemisphere at any one time?
slides.explanation: There are typically three to five of these narrow plumes in each hemisphere at any given time, yet between them they move most of the water vapour travelling north and south.
